lesson.title: From a Whiff of Epinephrine to a Burst of Glucose: Tracing the cAMP Pathway Start to Finish
lesson.summary: The cyclic AMP pathway, triggered when a hormone like epinephrine activates a G protein-coupled receptor, converts a brief hormonal signal into a sustained intracellular response by activating protein kinase A, which phosphorylates a specific set of target enzymes.
lesson.body:
The cyclic AMP pathway is one of the best understood signal transduction routes in biology, and it is worth tracing from beginning to end because each step illustrates a principle introduced earlier in this chapter. The pathway begins when a hormone such as epinephrine binds a beta adrenergic receptor, a G protein-coupled receptor found on the surface of liver, cardiac, and skeletal muscle cells. Binding causes the receptor to change shape and activate an associated stimulatory G protein, which exchanges GDP for GTP and separates into an active alpha subunit.

The GTP bound alpha subunit diffuses along the inner face of the plasma membrane and activates adenylyl cyclase, the membrane bound enzyme that converts ATP into the second messenger cyclic AMP. Because adenylyl cyclase is a catalyst, one activated enzyme molecule can generate many molecules of cyclic AMP over a short period, so cAMP concentration inside the cell rises quickly and substantially even though only a small number of hormone molecules bound receptors at the cell surface. This rise in cyclic AMP is the point at which the extracellular hormonal signal has fully become an intracellular chemical signal.

Cyclic AMP's main job in this pathway is to activate protein kinase A, often abbreviated PKA. Inactive PKA exists as a complex of two regulatory subunits and two catalytic subunits; when cyclic AMP molecules bind the regulatory subunits, they release the catalytic subunits, which are now free and enzymatically active. Active PKA is a kinase, meaning it transfers phosphate groups from ATP onto specific serine or threonine residues of target proteins, and it is not restricted to one target: it can diffuse through the cytoplasm and even enter the nucleus, phosphorylating a whole set of proteins appropriate to the specific cell type it is acting in.

In a liver cell, one especially well characterized set of PKA targets controls glycogen metabolism. PKA phosphorylates and activates an enzyme called phosphorylase kinase, which in turn phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase, the enzyme that breaks glycogen down into glucose-1-phosphate for release as glucose. At the same time, PKA phosphorylates and inhibits glycogen synthase, the enzyme that would otherwise build glycogen back up. The result is a coordinated shift toward glucose release rather than glucose storage, exactly the physiological response the body needs when epinephrine signals a fight or flight demand for readily available energy.

Like every signaling pathway covered in this chapter, the cyclic AMP pathway is fully reversible. The G protein alpha subunit hydrolyzes its own bound GTP and switches itself off, cyclic AMP is continuously broken down by the enzyme phosphodiesterase into inactive AMP, and protein phosphatases remove the phosphate groups PKA added to its targets, which is why caffeine, a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, prolongs cyclic AMP signaling and produces its stimulant effect. This entire route, receptor to G protein to adenylyl cyclase to cyclic AMP to PKA to target enzymes, is a direct, concrete illustration of the second messenger concept and sets up the next section's broader look at phosphorylation cascades, since the PKA step here is itself simply the first tier of a short kinase cascade.
